title: How AI Is Helping Legal Aid Serve 50% More Clients — Thomson Reuters AI for Justice Program One Year In
author: Laura Safdie · Pablo Ramirez

kp.k: Legal aid demand exceeds available staffing and funding
kp.d: The introduction frames the national justice gap as over 90% of civil legal needs going unrepresented. Ramirez provides an organizational example: in 2024, the Legal Aid Society of San Bernardino received over 26,000 requests, with nearly 15,000 or 16,000 calls unanswered. Its 45 staff members serve over 9,000 people annually. He presents AI adoption as a response to unmet demand and limited resources, rather than a strategy for reducing staffing.
qs: In the United States, over 90% of civil legal needs go unrepresented
So in 2024, we received over 26,000 requests, but nearly 15,000 or 16,000 of those calls went unanswered.
We're a small organization of 45 staff members serving over 9,000 people a year.

kp.k: Program combines access, tailored support and replication
kp.d: Safdie describes an initial group of 14 diverse legal services organizations receiving CoCounsel access and deeper implementation support. The program also offers special legal aid pricing to the broader community. Its mechanism is not simply software provision: Thomson Reuters works with practitioners to identify domain-specific tasks, overcome adoption barriers, document applications and develop replicable training.
qs: So in our initial version of the program, we had partnered really closely with 14 legal services organizations
we have special legal aid pricing for the broader legal aid community

It's not just here's a tool, go figure it out. It's here's a tool, here's training that's specific to your domain, here are proven use cases, and here's how we can partner to develop more use cases together.

kp.k: First-year reporting emphasizes time savings and increased capacity
kp.d: The introductory account reports attorneys saving up to 15 hours weekly, organizations serving as many as 50% more clients daily, and urgent case materials prepared up to 75% faster. Ramirez separately reports doubling urgent online calls and increasing full-representation cases. These are program and participant accounts; the document does not supply a measurement protocol or establish that each metric applies uniformly across the 14 organizations.
qs: attorneys are saving up to 15 hours per week, organizations are serving as many as 50% more clients daily, and urgent case materials are being prepared up to 75% faster.
It allowed us to double our urgent online calls. It allowed us to onboard more cases with full representation.

kp.k: AI accelerates drafting, research and evidence review
kp.d: Ramirez describes lawyers and paralegals using CoCounsel to draft motions and declarations, research cases, respond to opposing counsel and review voluminous evidence. His examples concern eviction and domestic violence matters, where faster preparation can make assistance available during a crisis. He attributes the ability to identify relevant threats and present evidence promptly to AI-assisted review.
qs: Instead of spending hours drafting declarations or doing research, they can turn around um half the time.
our attorney was able to leverage co-counsel to review all the material, voluminous material quickly.
they were able to quickly identify these different threats, the different evidence that allowed them to present it to the judge, which got them the protection.

kp.k: Efficiency supports representation and client contact
kp.d: Ramirez says time savings allow attorneys to listen to clients, provide advice sooner and undertake more courtroom representation. Safdie frames efficiency as a means to these human services, not an end in itself. The proposed restructuring is augmentation of legal aid staff: less preparation time and more direct advocacy, rather than replacing lawyers with automated advice.
qs: It's helped us, our attorneys do more, uh more of what they want to do, uh which is do that human interaction, stand by the client in court, do more of listening
The biggest impact I've seen before co-counsel are representations, meaning us being able to go to court to be next to the person and represent them was a lot lower. So we're able to increase it.
Efficiency isn't a goal. The goal is what efficiency allows you to do.

kp.d: Ramirez recounts a wrongfully evicted client regaining access to a home and a domestic violence client receiving protection after faster document preparation and evidence review. Safdie cites the Innocence Center's capacity to submit three times as many exoneration petitions explicitly as a proxy, not an exoneration count. Ambrogi qualifies discussion of outcomes by noting the many variables affecting case results.

kp.k: Reported benefits include reduced burnout and administrative burdens
kp.d: Safdie reports that more than 70% of respondents in surveys of the innovator class could devote materially more time to higher-value work, while more than half of attorneys reported reduced burnout and increased job satisfaction. She also highlights grant writing taking 30 minutes instead of a whole day as an example. Ramirez attributes improved retention and staff breathing room to the tool. These are reported survey responses and participant experiences; respondent counts and retention figures are not provided.

writing a grant application in 30 minutes instead of a whole day as an example.
more than half of the attorneys, even in this early stages of using AI are reporting a reduction in burnout and an increase in job satisfaction.
which increased our retention, avoided burnout.

kp.k: Human verification remains central to the adoption model
kp.d: Ramirez identifies confidentiality and accuracy as non-negotiable and says trust in CoCounsel's security and Westlaw and Practical Law sources informed selection. He states that attorneys remain involved and use expertise to check accuracy. Safdie distinguishes information-processing assistance that supports human decisions from higher-risk AI that supplants decision-making in sentencing, housing or university admissions, while acknowledging that AI bias is real.

our attorneys are never removed from this process. They're part of the process.
They use their expertise to ensure that this information is accurate.
you can use AI to supplant human decision-making, like in sentencing decisions, in housing decisions, in admissions for universities. And those are very high-risk uses of AI.

kp.k: Practical training and staff participation address adoption resistance
kp.d: Ramirez attributes staff acceptance to hands-on experience, involvement in the rollout, responsive support and discussion of objections rather than dismissing them. He recommends starting with small, low-risk applications and involving others in asking questions. Safdie identifies fragmentation across many small organizations, uneven technical capacity and fear of AI risks as obstacles requiring sustained education and outreach.

kp.k: Public playbooks aim to scale intensive implementation support
kp.d: Safdie says the program has developed over 100 use cases across at least a dozen practice areas and is publishing the material for legal aid organizations, including noncustomers. She nevertheless identifies scaling the depth of individual implementation support as an unresolved challenge. Planned expansion includes law firm pro bono teams, law school clinics and partnerships that disseminate practical knowledge; additional participants are being considered through rolling inbound interest rather than another formal application class.

kp.k: AI supplements funding and requires broader collective participation
kp.d: Ramirez argues that AI can expand services using existing resources while legal aid continues seeking funding and staff. Safdie warns that resource constraints could leave legal aid behind rapidly adopting law firms and corporate legal departments. Ambrogi argues that addressing the justice gap at scale requires more than one vendor or product; Safdie agrees that the program should provide a model for wider participation.

It's not a replacement for more staff. It's a force multiplier.
I'm seeing law firms and corporate legal departments adopt AI at such a rapid pace.
it can't be just one company. can't be just one product.

kp.k: Long-term justice-gap reduction remains an aspiration
kp.d: Safdie interprets first-year experience as validation of a scalable approach and expresses strong optimism about ethically applied professional AI, while acknowledging the program remains at an early stage. Ramirez is more cautious about fully closing a gap he says continues to grow. Safdie's suggestion of cutting unmet need in half is an illustration of potential impact, not a demonstrated result or dated forecast.

Will we ever bridge it? I don't think we will because it continues to grow.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Safdie and Ramirez describe AI as augmenting legal aid capacity, accelerating urgent work, improving staff sustainability and potentially reducing unmet legal need, rather than replacing lawyers.
pts.d: Ramirez attributes to CoCounsel savings of 15 hours per person per week, doubled urgent hotline capacity, faster drafting and responses to opposing counsel, and increased full representation. The article's introductory summary reports organizations serving as many as 50% more clients daily and urgent materials being prepared up to 75% faster; these are distinct from Ramirez's hotline claim. Ramirez says faster drafting and evidence review helped an evicted client return home and a domestic violence survivor obtain protection. Safdie says AI frees lawyers and paralegals for higher-value work, supports nonprofit administration, and reduces burnout. She cites the Innocence Center submitting three times as many exoneration petitions as a proxy for increased opportunity to obtain relief, not as an exoneration rate. Looking forward, Safdie presents ethically applied professional AI as a scalable model for more equitable legal assistance and predicts adoption may shift from whether to use AI to when and how. Ramirez warns that non-adoption risks leaving small legal aid organizations disadvantaged against larger organizations using the technology. Both describe reducing the justice gap as an opportunity, not a demonstrated nationwide result or a promise of its elimination.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers program surveys, participant-reported operational results and individual case accounts; its broader predictions rest on the speakers' interpretation of these early experiences.
pts.d: Safdie describes an initial group of 14 legal services organizations. She reports that more than 70% of surveyed participants could focus materially more on higher-value work and more than half of attorneys reported reduced burnout and increased job satisfaction. She gives a grant-writing example of 30 minutes rather than a full day. Ramirez supplies organizational experience from a 45-person organization serving over 9,000 people annually, including the reported time and capacity gains and accounts of eviction and domestic violence assistance. Safdie also offers the Innocence Center's petition volume as an outcome proxy. The document does not supply survey respondent counts, measurement protocols, comparison groups or systematic case-outcome data. The operational results are presented by a Thomson Reuters executive and a participating legal aid executive, rather than as independent benchmark findings. Predictions about widespread adoption, competitive disadvantage and closing the justice gap are attributed to their judgments and experience.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Results concern approximately the program's first year; wider effects are prospective and depend on training, human verification, suitable uses, resources and successful replication.
pts.d: The 2025 discussion concerns roughly one year after the program's launch. Its quantified gains describe early participating organizations, not a specified forecast for the legal aid sector. Safdie and Ramirez emphasize domain-specific training, responsive support, staff involvement, confidentiality, accuracy and human expertise. Ramirez explicitly says attorneys remain in the process and check accuracy, and recommends starting with low-risk tasks. Safdie distinguishes assistance with information and human decisions from higher-risk AI substitution for decision-making. Scaling deep support across fragmented, resource-constrained organizations remains an unresolved challenge. Plans include public playbooks, deeper existing partnerships and broader participation by pro bono teams and law school clinics; further use cases are envisaged over coming months and years as technology evolves. Neither speaker says AI removes the need for funding or staff. Ramirez doubts the growing justice gap will ever be fully closed; Safdie says eliminating it is probably not achievable in their lifetime and treats halving unmet need as an illustrative aspiration, not a timed prediction.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal beneficiaries described are under-resourced legal aid organizations, their lawyers and paralegals, and people who otherwise lack legal help.
pts.d: For lawyers and paralegals, the speakers describe less drafting, research and document-review burden, more time for listening and courtroom advocacy, reduced burnout and better retention. For executive directors and nonprofit managers, AI supports grant applications and organizational administration. For clients, claimed benefits include faster advice, greater access to full representation, earlier protection from domestic violence, restoration of housing and faster progress toward review of wrongful convictions. Housing, domestic violence, veterans' affairs and benefits work are among the practice areas discussed. Small organizations without technical staff are especially dependent on affordable access and implementation support. Pro bono lawyers and law school clinics are prospective expansion partners. Law firms and corporate legal departments appear as faster-adopting comparators, not as evidence that the legal aid program has generated equivalent gains across the commercial legal market.
